about: ONE table of owner vectors for common/test-leftovers.md section 3, run against BOTH implementations by tools/owner-conformance.test.mjs: owner_ok()/liveness() in tools/janitor.sh and parseOwner()/ownerState() in tools/lib/owned.mjs. Data only: nothing here is a test. Hosts are examples; no real machine names.

grammar.about: text is the content of an owner file or a lock reason as the reader sees it. valid=true means rule section 3's `<host>@<os>:<pid>[:<start>]` accepts it; valid=false means 'not exactly the form' (so the verdict is unknown, never gone). The rule fixes: host = no '@', no ':', no whitespace; os = exactly linux|macos|windows (lower case); pid and start = decimal digits; start optional; one line.

vectors.why: the smallest form: host, os, pid
two-field form on windows (the shape the plan gives: devbox@windows:37560)
three-field form with a start; macos is a legal os tag
an upper-case host is a legal host; section 3 compares hosts case-insensitively, so the grammar must not refuse it
dots in the host: only '@', ':' and whitespace are excluded
hyphen and underscore in the host
the writer ends its one line with a newline (writeOwner); a reader that refused it would refuse every claim
a CRLF line ending is still ONE line (a claim saved by a Windows editor)
pid 0 is digits, so the GRAMMAR accepts it; whether process 0 exists is a liveness question, not a grammar one
a 25-digit pid is digits; the rule sets no width. (It cannot name a process: liveness says gone, never live.)
leading zeros are still decimal digits
a start of 0 is digits
a non-ASCII letter in the host: the rule excludes only '@', ':' and whitespace
a very long start is digits; the rule sets no width
empty is not the form (a sweep reads an absent claim as unmarked, but the grammar itself refuses it)
the pid is not digits
the start is not digits
the pid is missing
four fields: at most host, pid, start
beos is not linux|macos|windows
no '@<os>' part (this is the shape of 'host:pid:start' from before section 3 named the os)
the host is empty
leading whitespace: not exactly the form
trailing space: not exactly the form
trailing tab: not exactly the form
a newline inside the os tag: the owner is ONE line
two lines: the owner is ONE line
the os tag is exactly lower case (linux|macos|windows); only the HOST comparison is case-insensitive
the os tag is exactly lower case
whitespace in the host
an '@' in the host
a ':' in the host
a trailing ':' leaves the start empty
an empty pid
a sign is not a digit
a sign is not a digit
a decimal point is not a digit
hexadecimal is not decimal digits
Arabic-Indic digits are not the decimal digits 0-9 the rule writes
git's own default lock reason names nobody (rule section 3: a lock that names nobody is unreadable)
the janitor's own placeholder for a claim it could not read
no pid at all
one line plus a blank line is not exactly the form; refusing it is the safe direction (unknown keeps the resource)
a no-break space is whitespace in Unicode; the rule excludes whitespace from the host
trailing garbage after the pid
the os tag is exactly one of three words, not a prefix of one
an exponent is not a decimal digit
whitespace inside the os tag
a carriage return with no line feed is no line end: it is not exactly the form (node rejects it; bash must too)
512 bytes is the longest claim a reader accepts
513 bytes is longer than any claim a reader accepts: unreadable, kept (bash reads 513 bytes to see it; node reads all of it)

hostnames.about: raw is a machine's DNS host name as the OS reports it; host is what an owner writes and what a reader compares: every maximal run of '@', ':' or whitespace becomes ONE '-', nothing is trimmed, the case is kept (the comparison itself is case-insensitive). node: hostName() in tools/lib/owned.mjs; bash: host_norm() in tools/janitor.sh. Hosts are examples.

vectors.why: a plain name is unchanged
a space becomes a dash
an '@' would end the host field of the owner
a ':' would split the owner's fields
a run of separators is ONE dash, not one per character
nothing is trimmed: a trailing separator becomes a dash
nothing is trimmed: a leading separator becomes a dash
the case is kept in what is written; readers compare case-insensitively
any whitespace, a tab too
dots stay: a DNS name keeps its labels
a no-break space is whitespace for node; bash must say so in any locale
a doubled dash in a name (punycode) is kept: only a run of separators collapses — `tr -s` would squeeze it
under WSL the host carries the distribution: distributions share one host name and one Docker daemon, but each has its own pid space
the distribution name is kept as it is, dots and dashes included
the distribution name is normalised by the same rule as the host
no distribution (not WSL): the plain host
a run of Unicode spaces is ONE dash too (narrow no-break space, ideographic space)

verdicts.about: owner + facts -> live | gone | unknown, per section 3's liveness procedure. host: same | same-case (this machine's name with the case swapped: compared case-insensitively) | foreign-name | foreign-os (this machine's name, another os tag: a Windows machine and its WSL share one name and have two pid spaces). pid: absent (no such process) | present | refused (the liveness query failed or was refused). startDelta: null = the owner carries no start, else owner.start - live start in seconds. liveStart: whether the reader can read the live process's start. pidText replaces the generated unmatchable pid with a literal pid text. ownerText replaces the generated owner with raw text ({HOST} = this machine's `<name>@<os>`, {NAME} = its name). tasklist=true: the vector also runs through the janitor's Windows branch (a stubbed tasklist), a representative subset because every janitor run spawns many processes. sides: which implementation can express the vector; the janitor never reads a start, so a vector whose verdict depends on a MISMATCH of two starts is node-only (section 3 lets a reader that cannot read the live start answer live); for those the janitor is held only to the safety property: it must not delete.

vectors.why: no process with that pid is the one answer that means gone
a start in the owner changes nothing when the pid is absent
alive, no start on either side: live (pid reuse then preserves)
alive, the owner carries a start but the reader cannot read the live one: live
alive, the owner carries no start: live even though the reader could read one
alive, equal starts: live
alive, starts 2 s apart: inside the tolerance (two seconds covers two one-second roundings)
alive, starts 2 s apart the other way: the tolerance is symmetric
alive, starts 3 s apart: a reused pid or a stepped clock, never proof of death and never proof of life
vectors.onlyNode: start comparison needs a live start the janitor does not read; the janitor answers live here, which also keeps the resource (checked by the safety test)

vectors.why: alive, starts 3 s apart the other way
vectors.onlyNode: start comparison needs a live start the janitor does not read; the janitor answers live here, which also keeps the resource (checked by the safety test)

vectors.why: a refused or failed query is never 'no such process'
a refused query with a start in the owner is still unknown
another machine: its pid says nothing here, so the process is NOT probed and the answer is unknown even though a probe would say absent
another machine, a pid that happens to exist here: unknown, not live
same machine name, other os tag: another pid space (Windows and its WSL), never probed
section 3 compares the host case-insensitively: this machine under another spelling is this machine
same, for a live pid
an owner that is not exactly the form is unknown, whatever the pid facts
git's default lock reason names nobody: unreadable, so unknown
a malformed start makes the whole owner unreadable even for a matching host and an absent pid
an unknown os tag is not this machine's, and not the form
four fields are not the form

pid 0 is digits (the grammar takes it) but names no process; a pid that cannot be a process says nothing, so it is never 'gone' (the 'no such process' answer is about a real pid that nothing holds). The stub ps answers 'no such process' for it, as ps -p 0 does on Linux

on Windows a bash started by a native process reports pid 1 for itself and its parent, and Windows has no pid 1: the process list has no row and process.kill says ESRCH, so a live CI job whose owner pid was taken from $PPID would read as gone. Pid 1 on a windows owner is unknown. (On any other machine this owner is another host's.)
a 25-digit pid cannot name a process and is not a safe integer; same reasoning as v23
